title: World Religions · Episode 4
chapters: Sikhism: the faith of the free kitchen
The Bahá'í Faith: one God, one humanity

units.t: World Religions. Episode four.
In this episode: Sikhism: the faith of the free kitchen, The Bahá'í Faith: one God, one humanity and The great pilgrimages.
Part one. Sikhism: the faith of the free kitchen.
Walk into any gurdwara in the world and someone will offer you a hot meal, no questions asked.
Here is the faith behind that open door.
A meal for anyone.
Picture a vast hall at the Golden Temple in Amritsar, India.
Rows of people sit cross-legged on long mats: farmers, tourists, businesspeople, the very poor.
Volunteers ladle out dal, vegetables and fresh roti.
Nobody pays, and nobody is asked their religion or caste.
On a busy day the kitchen serves tens of thousands of meals.
This is langar, the free community kitchen found at every gurdwara, or Sikh place of worship.
Sitting together on the floor is deliberate, because it puts everyone at the same level.
For Sikhs, langar is not charity handed down from above.
It is a practical way of living out equality.
Nanak's message.
Sikhism began in Punjab with Guru Nanak, born in 1469.
Tradition says he vanished into a river for three days and returned saying, 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim.'
Sikhs read this as a call to look past labels to a shared humanity and one God.
His teachings rejected empty ritual and the caste system.
The word Sikh means learner or disciple.
Sikhs believe in one formless God, expressed in the phrase Ik Onkar, 'One Creator'.
The aim of life is to move from ego towards God.
Three practices help: Naam Japna, remembering God, Kirat Karni, earning an honest living, and Vand Chakna, sharing what you have.
Ten Gurus, one book.
Guru Nanak was followed by nine more human Gurus over roughly two centuries.
The fifth, Guru Arjan, compiled the hymns of the Gurus and of some Hindu and Muslim saints into a single scripture.
Before his death in 1708, the tenth Guru, Gobind Singh, made a remarkable decision: there would be no more human Gurus.
The scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, would be the eternal Guru.
It is treated with deep respect.
In a gurdwara it rests on a raised platform under a canopy, someone waves a whisk over it, and at night it is carried ceremonially to its own resting room.
Visitors cover their heads and remove their shoes.
The Khalsa and Five Ks.
In 1699, at the spring festival of Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh created the Khalsa, a community of initiated Sikhs committed to discipline, courage and defending the vulnerable.

Members keep the Five Ks: kesh, uncut hair, kara, a steel bracelet, kanga, a small wooden comb, kachera, a cotton undergarment, and kirpan, a small ceremonial blade, a symbol of standing against injustice.
Uncut hair is covered by a turban, or dastaar, which many Sikhs see as a commitment to faith and dignity.
Many Sikh men take the surname Singh, lion, and many women Kaur, often 'princess'.
Shared surnames reject caste, since regional surnames often revealed it.
Sikhs in Australia.
Sikhs are not newcomers to Australia.
In the 1800s, Punjabi men worked here as hawkers and farm labourers, travelling the bush selling goods from carts.
The coastal town of Woolgoolga in northern New South Wales became home to a Punjabi farming community, and one of Australia's earliest gurdwaras was built there in the late 1960s.
Sikhism is now one of the fastest growing religions in the country, with more than 200,000 people identifying as Sikh in the 2021 census.
Worldwide there are around 25 to 30 million Sikhs, most of them in Punjab.
Many Australian gurdwaras cook langar for communities hit by bushfires and floods, carrying the free kitchen into new places.
The key idea: Langar, the free communal meal served at every gurdwara, is Sikh equality put into practice.
Part two. The Bahá'í Faith: one God, one humanity.
Born in nineteenth-century Persia amid persecution and exile, the Bahá'í Faith teaches that all the great religions come from the same source.
One of its temples stands among the gum trees of Sydney's northern beaches.
The Báb.
In 1844, in the Persian city of Shiraz, a young merchant named Siyyid ‘Alí-Muhammad declared himself the Báb, meaning "the Gate".
He taught that a new era of revelation was beginning and that he was preparing the way for a far greater messenger.
His message spread quickly, and so did opposition from religious and political authorities.
Thousands of his followers were killed.
The Báb was imprisoned and, in 1850, executed by firing squad in Tabriz.
Bahá'í accounts say the first volley only cut the ropes binding him, and a second regiment carried out the execution.
Bahá'ís regard him as a messenger of God in his own right and the forerunner of their faith's founder.
Bahá'u'lláh in exile.
Mírzá Husayn-‘Alí, born in 1817 to a noble Persian family, followed the Báb and took the title Bahá'u'lláh, "the Glory of God".
In 1852 he was thrown into a notorious underground prison in Tehran, the Black Pit, where Bahá'ís believe he first received the revelation of his mission.
He was banished to Baghdad, then Constantinople, Adrianople and finally the prison city of Akka, in what is now Israel.
In 1863, in a Baghdad garden called Ridván, he announced he was the messenger the Báb had foretold.
He wrote thousands of tablets and several books.
He died in 1892 near Akka, where his shrine is the holiest place on Earth for Bahá'ís.
Progressive revelation.
A central teaching is that there is one God, who has revealed truth to humanity in stages.
Messengers such as Abraham, Moses, Krishna, Zoroaster, the Buddha, Jesus and Muhammad are seen as teachers from the same divine school, each bringing guidance suited to their age.
Their spiritual truths are eternal, while their social laws suited particular times and places.
The Báb and Bahá'u'lláh are the most recent messengers, though not the last; Bahá'ís believe revelation will continue in the far future.
This leads them to treat other religions with deep respect, seeing divisions as the result of human interpretation rather than of the founders' teachings.
Unity and elected councils.
If there is one God and one unfolding religion, Bahá'ís reason, there is one human family.
From this come principles that sounded radical in the nineteenth century: equality of women and men, universal education, and ending prejudice of race, class, nation or religion.
True science and true religion cannot conflict, since both seek truth.
Bahá'u'lláh also called for world peace, global governance and an international auxiliary language.
There are no priests or ministers.
Since 1963 the faith has been governed by the Universal House of Justice, a nine-member council in Haifa.
Communities elect nine-member spiritual assemblies with no nominations, candidates or campaigning: each voter prays and writes the names of those best suited to serve.
Life centres on the Nineteen-Day Feast, as the calendar has nineteen months of nineteen days.
Temples and persecution.
Bahá'í Houses of Worship are nine-sided, crowned with a dome, and open to everyone.
Services are simple readings and prayers from many faiths' scriptures, often sung by a choir without instruments, with no sermons.
The lotus-shaped temple in New Delhi, completed in 1986, is one of India's most visited buildings.
Sydney's, in bushland at Ingleside, was dedicated in 1961.
The faith's holy places in Haifa and Akka were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.
The faith has spread to almost every country, with followers estimated in the millions.
In Iran, though, Bahá'ís are the largest non-Muslim minority and their religion is not recognised.
Since 1979, hundreds have been executed and many imprisoned, barred from university or stripped of property, according to the United Nations and human rights groups.
Bahá'ís have responded without violence.
The key idea: The Bahá'í story begins in 1844, when a young Persian merchant declared a new age and was later executed.
Part three. The great pilgrimages.
Every year millions of people walk, pray and queue for days to reach a single sacred place.
Pilgrimage is one of the oldest things humans do, and it is booming.
Why people make the journey.
A pilgrimage is a journey to a place believed to be holy.
People make it to fulfil a duty, give thanks, ask for healing or forgiveness, honour the dead, or simply be near something sacred.

Almost every major tradition has sites: Jerusalem for Jews, Christians and Muslims; Mecca for Muslims; the Ganges for Hindus; Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha is said to have awakened, for Buddhists; the Golden Temple at Amritsar for Sikhs.
The hardship is often part of the point.
Walking long distances, fasting or sleeping rough strips away daily comforts, and many pilgrims say the road changes them as much as the destination.
The Hajj.
The Hajj, one of the Five Pillars of Islam, is a duty for every Muslim who is physically and financially able.
It takes place over several days in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah, and in recent years has drawn between one and a half and two and a half million pilgrims.
Before arriving, pilgrims enter a state of ritual purity called ihram.
Men wear two plain, unstitched white cloths, so rich and poor stand alike before God.
Pilgrims circle the Kaaba seven times anticlockwise.
The most important moment is a day standing in prayer on the plain of Arafat.
They also throw pebbles at pillars in Mina, remembering Abraham's rejection of temptation.
Eid al-Adha follows, celebrated by Muslims worldwide.
Rivers and the Kumbh Mela.
Hindu tradition says gods and demons churned the cosmic ocean for amrita, the nectar of immortality.
Drops spilled from the pot, or kumbha, at four places: Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik.
The Kumbh Mela rotates among them, and the largest gatherings, at Prayagraj, draw tens of millions over several weeks.
Pilgrims believe bathing at auspicious times washes away sins.
Organisers build a temporary city with roads, bridges, hospitals and police stations.
UNESCO recognised the festival in 2017.
Varanasi, on the Ganges, is among the world's oldest continuously inhabited cities and is Shiva's city.
Many Hindus believe dying there, or having ashes placed in the river, brings moksha, release from rebirth.
Cremation fires at Manikarnika ghat burn day and night.
Camino and Shikoku.
According to tradition, the remains of St James were discovered in north-western Spain in the ninth century, and a cathedral rose at Santiago de Compostela.
Medieval pilgrims walked from all over Europe along the Camino.
The scallop shell became their symbol, and yellow arrows still guide walkers.
Hundreds of thousands now arrive each year; those who walk the final 100 kilometres, or cycle 200, can receive a certificate called the Compostela.
On Japan's island of Shikoku, a loop of about 1,200 kilometres links 88 Buddhist temples, honouring the monk Kūkai.
Pilgrims, called henro, wear white and carry a staff said to represent Kūkai walking beside them.
Walking it takes one to two months.
Locals offer pilgrims gifts of food or money, a custom called osettai.
Pilgrimage today.
Cheaper travel has transformed pilgrimage.
Journeys that once took months now take hours, and numbers have grown enormously.
That brings pressure.
Saudi Arabia allocates Hajj places by country through a quota and has built vast infrastructure to move crowds safely, yet crushes and extreme heat remain serious dangers at crowded sites.
Popular Camino routes face overcrowding, and towns worry about housing and daily life.
New kinds of pilgrimage have appeared too.
Many Australians and New Zealanders travel to Gallipoli for Anzac Day dawn services, and visitors file past the graves of musicians and writers.
Whether religious or not, people still seem to need special places where they feel connected to something larger than themselves.
The key idea: Pilgrimage joins an outer journey to an inner one, and the hardship is often part of the point.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why do people sit together on the floor to eat langar?
Answer. It puts everyone at the same level.
Question two. What did the Báb teach about his own role?
Answer. That he was a forerunner of a greater one.
Question three. What role does hardship play in pilgrimage?
Answer. It is often part of the journey's purpose.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
